Measuring National Income: The market value of all final goods and services produced domestically
A good purchased by its end user, counted in GDP
A good used to produce another good, excluded to avoid double counting
GDP as consumption plus investment plus government plus net exports
Household spending on goods and services
Business spending on capital, plus new housing and inventory change
Output valued at constant prices, removing inflation
The ratio of nominal to real GDP times one hundred
Output divided by population, a rough living-standard measure
It omits leisure, household work, inequality, and environmental cost
Measuring the Cost of Living: Consumer Price Index
A measure of the price of a fixed basket of consumer goods
Inflation rate
The percentage change in a price index over time
Base year
The reference year against which price levels are compared
Substitution bias
CPI overstating inflation because consumers switch to cheaper goods
Core inflation
Inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices
Deflation
A sustained fall in the general price level
Disinflation
A slowing in the rate of inflation, not falling prices
Indexation
Automatically adjusting a payment for inflation
Real interest rate
The nominal rate minus the inflation rate
Fisher effect
Nominal interest rates adjusting one for one with expected inflation
Purchasing power
How much a unit of currency can actually buy
Production and Growth: Productivity
Output produced per hour of labour
Physical capital
The equipment and structures used to produce goods
Human capital
The knowledge and skills embodied in workers
Natural resources
Inputs provided by nature, either renewable or nonrenewable
Technological knowledge
Society's understanding of the best ways to produce
Diminishing returns to capital
Each additional unit of capital adding less output
Catch-up effect
Poor countries growing faster from the same investment
Convergence
The tendency of income levels to move closer over time
Property rights and growth
Secure ownership encouraging investment and innovation
Brain drain
The emigration of skilled workers from developing countries
Sustainable growth
Growth that does not deplete the basis of future production
Saving, Investment, and the Financial Sy: The institutions matching savers with borrowers
A debt certificate promising interest and repayment of principal
A claim to partial ownership of a firm
An institution such as a bank channelling funds indirectly
A pooled investment holding many securities
Total income remaining after consumption and government purchases
Household income remaining after taxes and consumption
Negative public saving, when spending exceeds revenue
The market where saving supplies and investment demands funds
Government borrowing raising rates and reducing private investment
Spreading investments to reduce exposure to any single loss
Unemployment: Labour force
Everyone employed plus everyone actively seeking work
Unemployment rate
Unemployed as a share of the labour force
Labour force participation rate
The labour force as a share of the adult population
Discouraged worker
Someone who has stopped looking and is not counted as unemployed
Frictional unemployment
Short-term joblessness while matching workers to jobs
Structural unemployment
Joblessness from a mismatch of skills or location
Cyclical unemployment
Joblessness caused by a downturn in the business cycle
Natural rate of unemployment
The rate that persists even in a healthy economy
Minimum wage effects
A binding wage floor potentially raising unemployment for low-skill workers
Efficiency wages
Above-market pay used to raise productivity and reduce turnover
Job search
The process of matching workers with suitable positions
The Monetary System: Assets people regularly use to buy goods and services
Money's role as an accepted means of payment
Money's role as the yardstick for posting prices
Money's role in transferring purchasing power over time
Money with value by government decree rather than intrinsic worth
Money with intrinsic value, such as gold
The institution overseeing the banking system and money supply
The share of deposits a bank holds rather than lends
The amount of money the banking system creates per dollar of reserves
Buying or selling government bonds to change the money supply
Depositors withdrawing en masse, threatening a bank's solvency
Money Growth and Inflation: Quantity theory of money
The money supply determining the price level in the long run
Classical dichotomy
The separation of real variables from nominal variables
Monetary neutrality
The idea that money supply changes do not affect real variables long run
Velocity of money
How often a unit of currency changes hands in a year
Quantity equation
Money times velocity equals price level times output
Inflation tax
The erosion of currency value that funds government spending
Hyperinflation
Extremely rapid inflation destroying confidence in a currency
Shoeleather cost
Resources wasted reducing money holdings during inflation
Menu cost
The expense of frequently changing posted prices
Relative price variability
Distorted price signals caused by inflation
Unexpected inflation
Inflation that redistributes wealth from lenders to borrowers
Open-Economy Macroeconomics: Net exports
The value of exports minus imports
Trade surplus
Exporting more in value than a country imports
Trade deficit
Importing more in value than a country exports
Net capital outflow
Domestic purchase of foreign assets minus foreign purchase of domestic assets
Nominal exchange rate
The rate at which one currency trades for another
Real exchange rate
The rate at which goods of one country trade for goods of another
Appreciation
A currency gaining value against another
Depreciation
A currency losing value against another
Purchasing power parity
The theory that a currency should buy the same amount everywhere
Capital flight
A sudden large reduction in demand for a country's assets
Tariffs and trade policy
Restrictions that alter trade flows but not the overall trade balance
Aggregate Demand and Supply: Aggregate demand
The total quantity of output demanded at each price level
Wealth effect
A lower price level raising real wealth and consumption
Interest rate effect
A lower price level reducing rates and raising investment
Exchange rate effect
A lower price level weakening currency and raising net exports
Short-run aggregate supply
An upward-sloping curve reflecting sticky prices or wages
Long-run aggregate supply
A vertical curve at potential output, independent of the price level
Potential output
The output an economy produces at its natural rate of unemployment
Recessionary gap
Output below potential, with elevated unemployment
Inflationary gap
Output above potential, generating price pressure
Demand shock
A sudden shift in aggregate demand
Supply shock
A sudden shift in production costs, such as an oil price spike
Stagflation
Simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment from an adverse supply shock
Monetary Policy: Expansionary monetary policy
Increasing money supply and lowering rates to stimulate demand
Contractionary monetary policy
Reducing money supply and raising rates to slow inflation
Federal funds rate
The overnight interbank rate the central bank targets
Discount rate
The rate the central bank charges banks directly
Reserve requirement
The minimum share of deposits banks must hold
Liquidity preference theory
Interest rates set by money supply and demand in the short run
Transmission mechanism
The path by which rate changes reach spending and output
Zero lower bound
The constraint when rates cannot fall meaningfully below zero
Quantitative easing
Large-scale asset purchases used when rates are already near zero
Central bank independence
Insulation from political pressure to keep policy credible
Inflation targeting
Committing publicly to a specific inflation goal
Fiscal Policy: Expansionary fiscal policy
Raising spending or cutting taxes to stimulate demand
Contractionary fiscal policy
Cutting spending or raising taxes to cool the economy
Multiplier effect
An initial spending change generating larger total income change
Marginal propensity to consume
The share of an extra dollar of income that is spent
Crowding-out effect
Fiscal expansion raising rates and reducing private investment
Automatic stabilizer
A policy such as unemployment insurance that dampens cycles automatically
Discretionary policy
Deliberate policy changes requiring legislative action
Implementation lag
The delay between recognising a problem and policy taking effect
Structural deficit
The deficit that would remain at full employment
Debt-to-GDP ratio
National debt measured against the size of the economy
Ricardian equivalence
The idea that households save in anticipation of future taxes
The Phillips Curve: Phillips curve
The short-run inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment
Short-run Phillips curve
A downward-sloping trade-off at given inflation expectations
Long-run Phillips curve
A vertical line at the natural rate of unemployment
Natural rate hypothesis
The claim that unemployment returns to its natural rate regardless of inflation
Adaptive expectations
Expectations formed by extrapolating recent experience
Rational expectations
Expectations formed using all available information
Sacrifice ratio
The output lost per percentage point of inflation reduction
Disinflation policy
Deliberate contraction to bring inflation down
Credibility in policy
A trusted commitment reducing the cost of disinflation
Supply shock and the Phillips curve
An adverse shock shifting the curve outward
Economic Schools of Thought: Classical economics
The view that markets self-correct and money is neutral
Keynesian economics
The view that demand shortfalls can persist and warrant intervention
Monetarism
The view that money supply growth is the dominant driver of the economy
New classical economics
Models built on rational expectations and market clearing
New Keynesian economics
Models with rational expectations plus sticky prices and wages
Supply-side economics
The view that tax cuts on production drive growth
Austrian school
Emphasis on individual action, capital structure, and scepticism of intervention
Behavioral economics
Incorporating psychological realism into economic models
Say's law
The classical claim that supply creates its own demand
Liquidity trap
A situation where monetary policy loses traction at very low rates
